title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: New Buffalo blocks a storage yard for a data center project; locals gain breathing room on traffic and noise.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're starting with a clear win for residents in New Buffalo, where the township board just turned down a permit for a storage yard that would have supported a nearby data center.
That decision feels like it could ripple out. Why does blocking one storage facility matter so much when there are dozens of bigger proposals on the map?

Because these support sites are the hidden backbone. Without the yard, construction trucks and equipment staging get a lot harder, which directly cuts down on the noise and traffic residents were worried about in Berrien County.
So it's not just the main data center building anymore. It's everything that has to come with it.
Exactly. And New Buffalo's board listened to neighbors who said they didn't want their rural roads turned into industrial corridors.
How common is this kind of pushback now? We've seen rejections before, but is this becoming a pattern across the state?
It's picking up. Townships are realizing they can say no to the supporting pieces even when the big project is already in motion elsewhere.
What does that do to the developers' timelines and costs?
It forces them to find new locations or scale back, which adds months and money. Some projects are already adjusting routes because of these local stands.
And for the communities themselves, what changes on the ground? Fewer trucks means less wear on roads and quieter evenings, right?
Yes, and it keeps farmland and residential areas from being carved up for temporary industrial use that might stick around longer than planned.
We've talked before about how these facilities pull huge amounts of power and water. Does rejecting the yard help slow any of that strain locally?
It buys time. Without easy staging, the whole supporting network slows down, which gives the grid and water systems a bit more breathing room before new demand hits.
What happens next in New Buffalo or similar spots? Will developers try again with a different plan?
They might appeal or look for another site, but today's vote shows boards are willing to draw lines on the smaller pieces that make the big ones possible.
It also sends a signal to other townships that they don't have to approve everything that comes with a data center.
Right. And that ties into the bigger picture we're seeing statewide with tax breaks and moratorium fights.
Let's stay on New Buffalo for a second. How does this fit with the state quietly expanding those tax incentives that shield data centers from local property taxes?
The incentives make the projects more attractive to companies, but they also mean towns like New Buffalo lose out on revenue while still facing the infrastructure costs.
So residents pay higher electric and water rates down the line, but the tax base doesn't grow to help cover it?
That's the tension. The state is trying to lure investment, yet local officials are left with the bill for roads, emergency services, and grid upgrades.
And now with today's rejection, it looks like some communities are deciding the trade-off isn't worth it.
Exactly. It puts pressure on the state to either tighten the incentives or give towns more say in the deals.
What about the lawsuit from Raeden over the moratorium blocking their Gibraltar project? Does today's New Buffalo vote change anything there?
Not directly, but it shows the same local resistance that the moratorium was meant to address. The lawsuit claims the pause was illegal and could force compensation or reopen sites in Wayne County.
So if Raeden wins, we might see more pressure on places like New Buffalo to reconsider supporting infrastructure?
Possibly. It could create a legal back-and-forth where developers challenge every rejection.
Meanwhile, Ypsilanti Township is looking at its own move to block new transmission lines for a University of Michigan project. How does that connect?
It's the same playbook: using local authority over power delivery to slow things down and protect residents from rate hikes and farmland loss in eastern Washtenaw County.
And the recall efforts against officials who supported projects? Only one made the ballot so far.
Voters are frustrated, but the petition process is tough. Still, the fact that 28 officials faced bids shows how deep the anger runs in some areas.
What about the maps out this week showing 20-plus proposals? Does New Buffalo's decision change the picture there?

It highlights which sites are vulnerable. The trackers from Michigan Advance and Crain's show everything from Monroe to the U.P., and local rejections like this one can knock supporting pieces off the board.
Mason County was also talking yesterday about impacts on EMS and roads. Is that the kind of conversation more places will have after seeing New Buffalo?
Yes. Rural counties are starting to run the numbers on how these projects affect budgets and services before they get too far along.
And GenH's idea for using Morley Dam for on-site power? That might sidestep some fights but still hits water use in Mecosta County.
It shows developers looking for workarounds, but the core issues of local control and resource strain remain.
Saturday's rejection in another township over noise, traffic, and water sounds familiar. Is this wave of no votes the new normal?
It feels that way right now. More boards are listening to residents and saying the supporting infrastructure isn't automatic.
So what's the takeaway for listeners 30 or 60 miles away who aren't near any of these sites yet?
Even if you're not next door, new transmission lines and higher regional power demand can still hit your bills. These local decisions shape how fast that spreads.
And the state tax breaks make it harder for towns to negotiate better terms.
Right. The incentives reward quick moves by companies but leave communities with less leverage.
What should people watch for in the coming weeks?
More townships testing similar rejections, plus the outcome of that Raeden lawsuit and any new moratorium votes.
And the meetings tonight and tomorrow give residents a direct shot at weighing in.
Let's move to quick hits. First, Michigan quietly broadened those data-center tax breaks, shielding operators from most local property taxes for up to 12 years.
Big Rapids and other rural spots could lose millions while still dealing with higher utility costs. That seems like a raw deal for the towns.
It rewards companies for locating here but gives townships little room to ask for better community benefits.
Next, Raeden is suing over the moratorium that blocked its $500 million Gibraltar campus.
The company says the pause was illegal and wants compensation or the restrictions lifted in Wayne County.
That could reopen fights for residents who thought the issue was settled.
Data center backlash has also sparked recall bids against 28 officials, though only one made the November ballot.
It shows the depth of frustration even if the recall bar is high.
Ypsilanti Township is weighing a temporary ban on new transmission lines for the U-M project to buy time on rate hikes and farmland.
Direct action on the power side that could affect eastern Washtenaw County.
New maps from Michigan Advance and Crain's show 20-plus proposals statewide, linking them to higher bills and water strain.
Residents can see exactly which sites already have tax breaks or grid connections.
Yesterday Mason County discussed impacts on EMS, roads, and budgets from proposed centers.
Rural counties are starting to model the full cost before projects advance.
And GenH floated using Morley Dam for a self-powered data center in Mecosta County.
It might avoid some utility battles but still raises water questions.
Saturday another township rejected a server farm over noise, traffic, and water concerns.
Keeping that rural area clear for now.
Now for on deck. Tonight Lyon Township Planning Commission takes up Project Flex final site plan approval with residents opposing noise, water, and energy impacts.
Lenox Township is reviewing its data center ordinance and possibly extending a moratorium.
Madison Heights City Council considers a temporary data center moratorium resolution.
And the Planning Commission reviews a new site plan for the Verrus data center project.
Tomorrow Waterford Township Planning Commission looks at a six-month extension of its data center moratorium.
Plenty of chances for neighbors to show up and speak.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: New Buffalo Rejects Data Center Storage Yard as Communities Push Back on Infrastructure
